title: Storage in Kubernetes
summary: How persistent data survives in a system built to churn Pods constantly.

slides.markdown:
A **Volume** in Kubernetes is tied to the **Pod's** lifecycle, not any one container's. If a container in a Pod crashes and restarts, a Volume it was writing to survives untouched — but if the whole Pod is deleted (a reschedule, a rolling update), a plain `emptyDir` Volume is deleted with it.

That's the gap **PersistentVolumes** exist to close: storage that outlives not just a container, but the Pod itself, including reschedules onto an entirely different node.

slides.subTitle: The request/supply model
slides.markdown:
Kubernetes splits storage into a supply side and a demand side.

![PersistentVolume and PersistentVolumeClaim](assets/pv-pvc-model.svg)

A **PersistentVolume (PV)** is actual storage (a cloud disk, an NFS share) provisioned in the cluster. A **PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)** is a Pod's *request* — "give me 10Gi, ReadWriteOnce." Kubernetes binds a PVC to a matching PV; the Pod only ever references the PVC, keeping its spec portable across clusters.

slides.subTitle: StorageClasses and dynamic provisioning
slides.markdown:
Pre-creating PVs by hand doesn't scale. A **StorageClass** names a provisioner (e.g. a cloud provider's block storage driver) plus its parameters (disk type, encryption, replication). When a PVC references a StorageClass, the provisioner **dynamically creates** a matching PV on demand — no one pre-provisions anything.

Most clusters set a StorageClass as the default, so a PVC with no `storageClassName` still gets dynamically provisioned storage automatically.

Not every storage backend supports every access pattern.

| Mode | Meaning | Common backend support |
|---|---|---|
| RWO (ReadWriteOnce) | One node can mount read-write | Almost all block storage (EBS, GCE PD) |
| ROX (ReadOnlyMany) | Many nodes, read-only | Some network/file storage |
| RWX (ReadWriteMany) | Many nodes, read-write | Network filesystems (NFS, EFS, Filestore) — not typical block storage |

Asking for RWX on plain cloud block storage is a request that will never bind — that class of storage is fundamentally single-attach, no matter how the PVC is worded.

**The wrong belief:** "deleting a PVC is a safe, routine cleanup step."

**Why it breaks:** a PV's **reclaim policy** decides what happens to the underlying storage once its PVC is deleted. `Delete` (the common default for dynamically-provisioned storage) destroys the actual disk — permanently. `Retain` keeps the disk around, unbound, for manual recovery.

**The correct model:** for anything holding data you can't regenerate, explicitly set `Retain` (or take independent backups) — never assume the default reclaim policy matches what you'd want for that specific volume.

A StatefulSet's `volumeClaimTemplates` creates one PVC **per replica**, named to match the replica (`data-db-0`, `data-db-1`) — and that specific PVC reliably reattaches to that specific replica across restarts and rescheduling, unlike a Deployment where replicas are interchangeable.

Scaling a StatefulSet down doesn't delete its PVCs by default — they're kept so scaling back up returns the same replica to the same data, which is exactly the guarantee a clustered database needs.

slides.subTitle: Resizing a PVC without losing data
slides.markdown:
If the StorageClass has `allowVolumeExpansion: true`, edit the PVC's `spec.resources.requests.storage` to the larger size and apply it — the underlying volume is expanded by the CSI driver in place, with the data untouched. Depending on the filesystem/driver, the Pod may need a restart for the filesystem itself to see the new size, but the volume is never recreated from scratch.

Without `allowVolumeExpansion` on the StorageClass, resizing isn't possible at all — that flag has to be set before the PVC is created, not after the fact.
